# Stings, bites and ticks

Summer reference sheet for the trail, the garden and the beach.

## Bee and wasp stings

Scrape the stinger out sideways with a fingernail or a card; do not squeeze it. Wash the area, put a cold pack on it for 10 minutes, and take an oral antihistamine for itching. Swelling that spreads over a day or two is common and is not an allergy.

## Allergic reactions to stings

Hives away from the sting, swelling of the face, lips or tongue, wheezing, dizziness or vomiting mean a serious allergic reaction. Call 911. If the person has a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, use it at once, in the outer thigh, and then call anyway: the symptoms can come back.

## Removing a tick

Use fine-tipped tweezers and grasp the tick as close to the skin as you can. Pull straight up with steady, even pressure. Do not twist or squeeze it, and do not smother it with petroleum jelly or nail polish or touch it with a hot match: these make it release more of its saliva. Wash the bite and your hands, and keep the tick in a sealed bag. Watch for a rash or fever over the next 30 days.

## Spider bites

Most spider bites are harmless: wash, apply a cold pack and watch the area. Go to the emergency department for severe pain, an expanding ulcer or a dark blister, or muscle cramps after a bite from a black widow or a recluse.

## Mosquito and flea bites

Itching eases with a cold cloth, hydrocortisone cream or an oral antihistamine. Scratching leads to infection; keep nails short.

## Animal bites

Wash a dog or cat bite with soap and running water for 5 minutes, cover it, and see a doctor the same day, because bites often need antibiotics and sometimes a rabies assessment. A bite from a bat, or from any wild animal, needs medical advice at once.
